summary: All four round-1 findings are genuinely fixed. F1 verified against the code, not the prose: Accumulator.adaptInterval's middle band IS the else branch -- it sets lowStreakStartMillis = -1 and highStreakStartMillis = -1 and never touches currentInterval, so 0.4 < r < 0.9 holds whatever interval is in force; and the high band with DEFAULT_INTERVAL_SHORTEN_DELAY = Duration.ZERO does collapse to intervalFloor on the same drain (nowMillis - highStreakStartMillis == 0 >= 0), exactly as the ADR and the SPEC now warn. The arithmetic checks out: 1000 x 228 B = 228,000 B = ~223 KiB/chunk; 228,000/5 s = 45,600 B/s (~44 KB/s); the 0.4-0.9 band against DEFAULT_MAX_SEGMENT_BYTES = 8 MiB is 15 producers (0.408) to 33 (0.897), so '15 to 33' is right; 24 gives 5,472,000 B = 5.22 MiB and fillRatio 0.652, the exact midpoint of the two thresholds; aggregate 1.044 MiB/s, which is criterion 4's worked load as claimed; 200 MiB / 5.472 MB = 38.3 flushes x 5 s = ~192 s. F2's ~13.4 MB/s is 0.4 x 8 MiB / 0.25 s = 13,421,773 B/s, correct, and the justification is now non-circular and independently checkable: ADR-0017 line 21 does price the 6-writers-@-5s / 1 MiB/s-per-pod point at $15.55/mo, so the criterion-4 load really is the designed steady state, and the roadmap row exists, is well-formed and carries the same numbers. F3's corrections are arithmetically right (2,097,174/10 = 209,717 B is the measured 10-flush average with its ~198-record tail; the full-chunk figure is 228,000 B) and the ADR keeps the measured 40.7 KB/s explicitly distinguished from the derived steady state. F4's replacement line is accurate: R1b is defined in docs/internal/standards/cost.md:11 and nowhere in 02-cost-model.md; dropping Research: is correct since the adr skill makes it conditional and this finding came from measurement, and ADR-0022 sets the precedent for citing a cost rule in the header. The ADR still meets the skill: five rejected alternatives, each with a number. The cost lens is clean -- one PUT plus one commit delta per flush, unchanged cadence, and 24 producers bundle into ONE accumulator, so request rate still scales with flushes and not with producers, records, shards, partitions or indices. Four minors, none blocking, all recordable rather than fixable per rule 11: the backlog row still carries the pre-fix figures in its own narrative, the ADR's forward reference names the wrong file, nothing says how the interval gets warmed to the ceiling before the 24 producers start (and the obvious reading is impossible), and the one carried-forward option that is not cost-neutral is not marked as such.

findings.title: F3's numeric correction was applied to the ADR and the SPEC but not to the backlog row's own narrative, which now states both figures as fact
findings.failure_scenario: The M3.6 row asserts 'a 200 MB single-producer body at the ceiling would take ~86 minutes' and 'a blocking producer never has more than one ~210 KB chunk outstanding', then closes by saying the corrected figures are ~223 KB and ~79 min. Both cannot be true: 209,715,200 B / (228,000 B per 5.15 s) = 4,736 s = 78.9 min, so ~86 min is the superseded number the same row says was wrong. A reader harvesting numbers at the milestone boundary (review.md rule 13) reads backlog.md, not the ADR, and takes ~86 min and ~210 KB/chunk forward. Note the measured description -- '10 flushes, 5.15s each, ~210 KB each = ~40 KB/s' -- is accurate for the MEASURED run (2,097,174/10 = 209,717 B; /51.5 s = 40.7 kB/s) and should stay; it is the derived ~86 min and the steady-state '~210 KB chunk' that are stale.

findings.title: The F2 fix's forward reference points at backlog.md, but the obligation was actually carried in roadmap.md -- and a backlog row for a later milestone cannot exist by backlog.md's own scope rule
findings.failure_scenario: The Decision section says 'Carried as a backlog row for a later milestone, not closed by this ADR -- see Consequences', while Consequences (line 166-168) and the actual change put it in roadmap.md's 'Deferred into a later milestone' table. AGENTS.md defines backlog.md as 'the current task list, authoritative, current milestone only', so a future reader chasing the accepted limitation greps backlog.md for a row that by construction will never be there, concludes the obligation was dropped, and either re-derives the ~44 KB/s cap from scratch or treats it as unrecorded. One word ('roadmap row') closes it.

findings.title: Nothing says how the interval reaches the ceiling before the 24 producers start, and the obvious reading is impossible -- with blocking producers fillRatio is interval-independent, so the middle band that HOLDS the ceiling is also what prevents ever reaching it
findings.failure_scenario: This ADR's own central finding is that a blocking producer advances exactly one chunk per flush. It follows that N blocking producers deliver exactly N chunks per flush REGARDLESS of the interval, so 24 producers sit at fillRatio ~0.65 at the 250 ms floor just as much as at the 5 s ceiling. Accumulator's constructor sets currentInterval = config.intervalFloor() for every instance, and adaptInterval's else branch (the middle band) leaves currentInterval untouched -- so a test that starts 24 concurrent producers under IngestConfig.defaults never leaves 250 ms, and runs its whole length in M1.18's floor regime while AC5's prose says 'the interval warmed to its 5 s ceiling'. That is round-1 F1's failure mode in a new dress: a green T12 that proves what M1.18 already proved. Reaching the ceiling needs a separate warm-up -- a lone low-fillRatio producer for the full DEFAULT_INTERVAL_LENGTHEN_DELAY of 2 minutes (which the ADR itself shows works: 0.026 fillRatio, low band), or a non-default lengthen delay -- and neither the ADR, AC5 nor the T12 row names one, nor is the ~120 s counted in the '~192 s (38 flushes)' claim at line 153 (still within M1.18's 480 s @Timeout at ~317 s total, so this is a test-design gap, not an infeasibility). Not major because AC5 does state 'warmed to its 5 s ceiling' as a precondition, so a floor-only run violates the criterion as written rather than satisfying it -- but the mechanism is the one thing an implementer cannot derive from the band arithmetic given. Related and worth recording in the same place: the band arithmetic uses BODY bytes (~228 B/record), while M3.2 measures fillRatio on the serialised segment length. For M1.18's fixture the action line is parsed away and not stored, so the per-record segment cost is ~216 B (1 flag + 5 + ~7 id + 10 version + 5 + 188 payload), giving 24 producers ~5.18 MB and fillRatio ~0.62, with the true band ~16-34 producers rather than 15-33. The conclusion is unchanged -- 24 is centred either way -- but M3.5 should not assert '=0.65' with a tight tolerance.

findings.title: The carried-forward option 'shorten the interval on a blocked producer' is a 20x PUT-rate change, and neither the ADR's rejection nor the roadmap row says so -- they treat it as equivalent to the cost-neutral option beside it
findings.failure_scenario: The ADR's 'Cost impact: none' is correct for the decision actually made, but it is stated 178 lines after two options are carried forward, one of which is not cost-neutral at all. A blocked-producer input to the control loop drives the interval toward the floor precisely while a large upload is in flight, which is ADR-0017's own priced comparison: 6 writers @ 250 ms = 24.00 objects/s = $311.04/mo against 6 writers @ 5 s = 1.20 objects/s = $15.55/mo, i.e. the 95%-of-the-saving dial this project exists to hold. Pipelined chunk appends, by contrast, change no flush cadence and are genuinely cost-neutral. The roadmap row lists both as 'each need their own measurement first', so whoever picks the obligation up in a later milestone starts by measuring producer throughput and can reach an implementation before anyone recomputes the bill -- the failure this repo's non-negotiable 6 and R1b exist to prevent. One clause naming the 20x on the blocked-producer option would close it.
